text: When several Business Rules apply to the same save, something has to decide the order they run in. This lesson covers the real order field, the overall sequence a save goes through from start to finish, and a table-inheritance behavior that catches a lot of new developers off guard.

The order field is just a number, and lower order runs first. Here, two before-update rules both touch the incident's urgency field. The rule at order 100 runs completely, start to finish, before the rule at order 200 even begins. Leave order at its default, and you're letting the platform decide something you should be deciding yourself.

Across an entire save, the sequence is fixed. First, every applicable before rule runs, in order. Then the actual database write happens. Then every applicable after rule runs, in order. And finally, any applicable async rules are queued to run later, in the background. Display rules sit completely outside this chain, since they run on form load, not on save.

Now the inheritance behavior. Incident, Problem, and Change Request all extend a base table called task. That inheritance isn't just a schema detail — it applies to Business Rules too. A rule written directly on task, with no table-specific scoping, runs for every table beneath it. This script checks sys class name specifically so its incident-only logic doesn't leak into Problem or Change.

That's genuinely useful when the logic really is universal — write it once on task, and every extending table benefits automatically. But it's exactly as dangerous when the logic is NOT universal. Skip that sys class name check, and a rule meant only for incidents quietly starts rewriting Problem and Change records too.

Order and inheritance both shape what actually runs, and when. Next, we'll look at the current and previous objects themselves — how to read a record's live values, and how to detect exactly what changed from its state before the save.
